Module 01 · 4 contact hours
01

Introduction to Artificial Intelligence

Concepts, Domains, and Applications

What people mean by "intelligent", what this field actually builds, and the responsibility that comes with it.

Before we write a single algorithm, we should agree on what we are trying to build. This module is the map of the whole course: what AI means, where it came from, what it can and cannot do today, and what we owe the people who will use our systems.

Learning objectives

  • Describe what makes a system "artificially intelligent", and recognize one when you see it.
  • Distinguish an agent from an intelligent agent, and give an example of each.
  • Explain, from the history of AI, why a system's abilities and limits should be described precisely.
  • Name the main areas of AI and give a real application for each.
  • Discuss the responsibilities that come with building systems whose predictions and decisions affect people.

Key terms in this module

Artificial Intelligence (AI)
A branch of Computer Science concerned with building systems that perform tasks associated with intelligence. This course emphasizes the rational agent view: systems that perceive their environment, make decisions, and act to achieve goals.
Agent
A system that perceives its environment and acts upon that environment. A thermostat, an automatic door, a robot, or a program that acts on websites, files, or people can all be agents.
Environment
What lies outside the agent and can affect it or be affected by its actions: a room or a road for a robot; websites, files, databases, other programs, or people for a software agent.
Computation
Turning inputs into outputs without perceiving or acting on an outside environment, such as a formula that only recalculates its own sheet.
Intelligent agent
An agent that perceives its environment, makes decisions, and takes actions to achieve goals.
Rational
Choosing the action expected to give the best performance, given what the agent has perceived and knows. Module 2 makes this precise. Rational does not mean perfect, and it does not mean always successful.
Turing test say: TOO-ring
A test proposed by Alan Turing in 1950: a judge exchanges written messages with a hidden human and a hidden machine. If the judge cannot reliably tell which is which, the machine passes.
Machine Learning (ML)
A subfield of AI in which systems learn patterns from data to improve at a task, rather than relying only on explicitly programmed rules.
Deep Learning
A subfield of machine learning based on neural networks with multiple layers that learn representations from data.
Generative AI say: GenAI
An area of AI focused on generating new content — text, images, audio, video, or code — from patterns learned in data.
Expert system
An AI system that uses knowledge and rules collected from human experts to reason about problems in one specific domain.
NLP say: Natural Language Processing
A subfield of AI concerned with enabling computers to process, understand, and generate human language, in text and in speech — including Arabic.
AI winter
A period of sharply reduced interest, investment, and funding in AI, following unmet expectations and limits in the technology of the time.
AGI say: Artificial General Intelligence
Intelligence across tasks, comparable to a human's. No system today is agreed to have it.
LLM say: Large Language Model
A model trained on very large amounts of text, able to read and generate language. Today's chat assistants are built around one.
Narrow AI
AI built for one job or one limited domain, rather than having general-purpose intelligence comparable to a human.
Bias
A systematic pattern in a system that can lead to unfair or unequal outcomes. It can arise from the data, the system design, the objective it was given, or the way it is used.
Data minimization
Collecting only the personal data a system actually needs, and keeping it only as long as it is needed.
Section 1.1

What is Artificial Intelligence?

Ask ten researchers to define artificial intelligence and you will get ten answers. This is not because the field is confused. It is because intelligence itself is hard to define.

Think about a calculator and a mobile map app

A calculator multiplies faster than any human. Nobody calls it intelligent.

Your map app chooses a route around a traffic jam on King Abdulaziz Road, changes its mind when an accident appears, and gets you home. We are happy to call that intelligent.

So the difference is not speed, and it is not the amount of calculation. The calculator wins on both. The difference is what the map app does with the situation it finds itself in.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a branch of Computer Science concerned with building systems that perform tasks associated with intelligence: perceiving, reasoning, solving problems, understanding language, making decisions, and acting in an environment.

There is no single agreed definition. Russell and Norvig organize the main ones around two questions: does the system think or act? And does it do so like a human or rationally? (Section 1.7 lays the four out, for those who want them.)

In this course we place particular emphasis on the rational agent view: intelligent systems perceive their environment, make decisions, and act to achieve goals. It is the foundation of most of what you will study here — search, optimization, games, constraint solving, and logical reasoning — and it remains the frame for modern AI agents too.

The idea behind everything in this course

An intelligent system can perceive a situation, consider what to do, and take action towards a goal. Hold on to those three words. The next section turns them into the one technical term this whole course is built on.

5 min read

Section 1.2

Agents, and intelligent agents

To understand AI from the agent perspective, we first need to understand what an agent is.

An agent is a system that perceives its environment and acts upon that environment.

The environment is what lies outside the agent and can affect it or be affected by its actions. For a robot, this may be a room or a road. For a software agent, it may be websites, files, databases, other programs, or people.

!
Where is the line?

A spreadsheet formula that only recalculates values inside its own sheet is better viewed here as a computation, not an agent. If the same spreadsheet watches for new data and sends an email when a condition is met, we can view it as an agent interacting with an external environment.

Calling a system an agent is a way of looking at it — a useful perspective for understanding what the system does.

Notice what the definition does not say: nothing about robots, code, or hardware.

Is every agent intelligent?

No.

A door that opens when someone steps in front of it perceives and acts. It is an agent. But it makes no choice — one input, one fixed response, forever. Nothing in it decides anything.

An intelligent agent is a system that perceives its environment, makes decisions, and takes actions to achieve goals.

Perceive and act make an agent. Deciding, towards a goal, makes it intelligent.
!
When do we call an agent intelligent?

Not every agent needs to be intelligent. Some agents simply follow fixed rules; others must choose their actions according to the situation and the goal. Both are agents, and both are useful — this course focuses on the second kind.

A quick test you can apply to any system: does it choose between options in order to reach a goal? Module 2 makes the idea of choosing well precise, under the name rationality.

Back to our definition

In section 1.1 we said that this course places particular emphasis on the rational agent view. At that point the words were not yet available. Now that agent, intelligent agent, and goal each have a precise meaning, we can state it properly:

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a field of Computer Science concerned with the study and design of intelligent agents — systems that perceive their environment, make decisions, and take actions to achieve goals.

This is the same field described in section 1.1, said in the language of this course. Every word in it is now a term you know — which is exactly why we took this order.

!
What about learning?

Some intelligent agents also learn — they improve their own decisions from experience. Learning is a powerful capability an agent may have; it is not part of what makes it an agent. The route planner of Module 3, the game player of Module 5, and the timetable solver of Module 6 all decide well and never learn anything. Module 2 shows exactly where learning fits: not as a separate way of choosing actions, but as an ability that can be added to any agent design.

One sentence to carry through the course

An agent perceives and acts. An intelligent agent perceives, decides, and acts towards a goal. AI studies and designs intelligent agents. If you remember nothing else from this module, remember that.

6 min read

Section 1.3

Agents come in different forms

The definition said nothing about hardware. That was deliberate — an agent does not have to be a robot, and the same three words describe very different systems.

💻 Software agent

Acts inside a digital environment. A fraud checker perceives a transaction, decides whether it fits your normal behaviour, and acts by approving it or asking you to confirm.

🤖 Robot agent

Acts in the physical world. A warehouse robot perceives shelves and obstacles through its sensors, decides on a route, and acts by moving.

🗣️ LLM-based agent

Uses a language model to read a request, decide which steps and which tools or APIs are needed, and carry them out — searching, writing a file, sending a message.

i
From classical agents to AI agents today

The idea of an agent is not new. What has changed is how one can be built. Classical agents relied on rules, search, planning, and logic. A modern AI agent may combine a language model with memory, tools, retrieval, planning, and feedback.

The technology changed; the question did not: given what the agent knows, what should it do next to reach its goal? That question is what this course is about.

!
Automation is not the same as an agent

Workflow platforms (Zapier, Make, n8n and others) are a common place to build systems that look intelligent. But a workflow with fixed steps — "when a form arrives, add a row, then send an email" — perceives and acts without ever deciding. It is an agent, not an intelligent one. A fixed workflow follows the steps you designed in advance; an intelligent agent chooses what to do next from its goal and the situation in front of it.

Check yourself

Which of these are agents, and which of those deserve to be called intelligent? (a) A washing machine that weighs the clothes and picks a water level. (b) A spreadsheet of student grades. (c) A map app rerouting around traffic.

Show answer

(a) An agent, but not an intelligent one: it perceives weight and acts on the water valve, yet it reads one number off a fixed table and never weighs alternatives. (b) Not an agent at all: it stores data and never acts on any environment. (c) An agent, and clearly an intelligent one: it perceives changing traffic, decides between routes whose outcomes it cannot fully predict, and acts towards the goal of getting you home.

A useful habit with borderline cases: ask what the system would do if the situation changed. If the answer is "exactly the same thing", there was no decision in it.

4 min read

Section 1.4

A very short history: hope, winter, hope again

AI is about seventy years old. Its history is a repeating cycle: a breakthrough, big promises, disappointment, then a quiet period of real work.

  1. 1950 — the question

    Alan Turing asks whether machines can think, and proposes his test: a judge exchanges written messages with a hidden human and a hidden machine; if the judge cannot reliably tell which is which, the machine passes.

  2. 1956 — the field gets a name

    A summer workshop at Dartmouth College gives "artificial intelligence" its name. The mood is very optimistic.

  3. 1956–1974 — early success, then the first winter

    Programs prove theorems and play simple games. But they struggle with realistic problems: the number of possibilities explodes — the problem you will meet in Module 3 — and computers are slow. Funding collapses in the mid-1970s: the first AI winter.

  4. 1980s — expert systems

    Industry buys systems full of human expert rules. They work well in narrow areas, but they are expensive to update and cannot learn. A second winter follows in the late 1980s.

  5. 1990s–2000s — learning from data

    The field turns to statistics and machine learning. In 1997 Deep Blue beats the world chess champion — using search, with alpha-beta pruning, which is Module 5.

  6. 2012 onwards — deep learning

    Big data, powerful GPUs, and deep neural networks transform vision and speech.

  7. 2017 onwards — the Transformer and large language models

    A new architecture, the Transformer, leads to large language models (LLMs), which read and write language far better than earlier systems. Generating text, not only classifying it, becomes part of everyday tools.

i
What this history teaches you

AI winters had several causes: limited computing power, scarce data, problems that proved harder than expected, and expectations that exceeded what the systems could actually deliver. One pattern is worth noticing: success in a narrow domain can raise expectations of much broader intelligence.

The lesson is simple: doing one task well is not general intelligence.

So be precise about what a system can do, what it cannot do, and the conditions it needs. Say "this model recognizes five diseases across three plant species from clear images", not "our AI diagnoses plant diseases" — good practice means being clear about capabilities and limitations.

بالعربية

كان لفترات تراجع الذكاء الاصطناعي (AI Winters) أسبابٌ متعدّدة، منها محدودية القدرة الحاسوبية، وقلّة البيانات، ومشكلاتٌ تبيّن أنها أصعب مما كان متوقّعاً، إضافةً إلى توقّعاتٍ تجاوزت ما كانت الأنظمة قادرةً فعلياً على تقديمه. وهناك نمطٌ يستحقّ الانتباه: النجاح في نطاقٍ ضيّق قد يرفع التوقّعات إلى ذكاءٍ أوسع بكثير.

والدرس بسيط: إتقان مهمّة واحدة لا يعني امتلاك ذكاءٍ عام.

لذلك كن دقيقاً عند وصف قدرات أيّ نظام: وضّح ما الذي يستطيع فعله، وما الذي لا يستطيع فعله، والظروف التي يحتاجها ليعمل كما هو متوقّع. فبدلاً من القول: «نظام الذكاء الاصطناعي لدينا يشخّص أمراض النباتات»، قل: «يتعرّف هذا النموذج على خمسة أمراض في ثلاثة أنواع نباتية من صورٍ واضحة». فالممارسة الجيدة تعني الوضوح بشأن قدرات النظام وحدوده.

The classical methods did not die

It is easy to think that deep learning replaced everything older. It did not. Your maps app still runs search. Airline and exam schedules still run constraint solving. Leading chess engines still use alpha-beta search. Modern systems can combine a learned part with a classical part — which is exactly why this course teaches you the classical half properly.

Section 1.5

The map of the field

AI is a broad field with several areas that often overlap. Here are the main ones you will meet in this course.

Areas of AI

🔍 Search and planning

Finding a sequence of actions that reaches a goal, or the best choice among many possibilities: routes, schedules, robot plans. Modules 3 to 6 of this course.

🧠 Knowledge and reasoning

Storing facts and deriving new ones. Expert systems and formal checking. Module 7.

📈 Machine learning

Learning patterns from data instead of hand-written rules: predictions, recommendations, fraud detection.

🗣️ Natural language processing

Processing and generating human language. Arabic brings its own challenges: rich word forms, missing short vowels, and many dialects.

👁️ Computer vision

Understanding images and video: medical scans, quality checks in factories, reading plate numbers.

🤖 Robotics

Agents with a body: warehouse robots, inspection drones, self-driving vehicles.

✨ Generative AI

Generating new content — text, images, audio, video, or code — from patterns learned in data. Most of today's generative systems are built with deep learning, and the area overlaps with NLP, computer vision, and speech.

This course covers the first two areas — search and planning, and knowledge and reasoning. The others have their own courses in the programme.

Where you can see it around you

🕋 Hajj and Umrah operations

Crowd density analysis from cameras, and planning walking routes and time slots for very large numbers of pilgrims.

🏦 Banking

Your bank app decides in milliseconds whether a transaction looks normal for you, and asks for confirmation when it does not.

🏥 Hospitals

Vision models mark suspicious areas on X-rays so the radiologist looks there first. The doctor still decides.

🛢️ Industry and energy

Predicting when a pump or turbine will fail, so maintenance happens before the breakdown.

🎓 Universities

Building exam timetables, spotting students at risk of dropping a course, and answering admission questions automatically.

📱 Arabic language tools

Speech recognition, translation, and assistants that must handle both formal Arabic and everyday dialect.

Each application above is an example of narrow AI: a system built for one job or one limited domain. A model that reads X-rays cannot book a flight. General intelligence across tasks — often called AGI — is a much stronger claim than doing many tasks well, and whether anything today is approaching it is still argued over.

Check yourself

A language model can write essays, translate between languages, and produce working code. Does doing many tasks make it general intelligence?

Show answer

Breadth of tasks is not the same thing as general intelligence. A system trained on an enormous amount of human text can do many tasks partly because many tasks appeared in that text. That is a real change from the narrow systems of ten years ago — but it is not automatically the same kind of capability a person has.

Three questions are more useful than the label itself. Can it transfer — meet a genuinely new kind of problem, unlike anything it was trained on, and still work it out? Can it learn a new domain from a handful of examples, the way you learn a new game from one explanation? Does it know its own limits, and say so, instead of answering confidently anyway?

Researchers disagree about where today's systems sit on these three, and that disagreement is honest rather than settled. What is not in dispute is the reasoning: counting tasks is weak evidence, because it measures coverage, not capability.

Section 1.6

Your responsibility when building AI systems

You are learning to build systems that make predictions, recommendations, and decisions that can affect people. A system does not have to act on its own to change someone's life — a score, a ranking, or a suggestion is enough. That reach is what creates the duty, and this is not a side topic: it is one of the official learning outcomes of this course.

Think like an engineer, not just a coder

Nobody builds a bridge and says "it held in the test, let's see what happens."

A coder asks: does the system work? An engineer also asks: what could go wrong, who could be affected, and what do we do when it fails?

When a system can affect people's lives, building it responsibly is part of the job — not something added after the code is finished.

Four questions to ask about any system you build

  1. Who could this system treat unfairly? bias & fairness

    A learning system reflects the patterns in the data it was trained on — including the unfair ones. An Arabic speech model trained mostly on one dialect may perform poorly for speakers of other dialects. A hiring filter trained on past hiring repeats the past, including its mistakes. That is one form of bias. Bias can come from the data, from the way the system is designed — which features you use, how the examples are labelled, what you tell it to maximize — or from how it is later used.

  2. Can I explain its decisions? explainability & transparency

    If your system recommends denying someone a loan or a university place, that person deserves a reason — whoever signs off on the decision. "The model said so" is not a reason. Some methods are easier to interpret — logic rules and decision trees show you the path they took. Others are much harder, and then the explanation has to be designed in from the start, not added at the end.

  3. What data am I collecting, and do I need it? privacy & data protection

    Ask this before the first record is stored, not afterwards. Personal data should be collected only when it is needed, kept only as long as it is needed, and protected while you hold it. The principle has a name worth knowing: data minimization — collect only what you actually need. Collecting "everything, just in case" is a risk you create for your users and then carry yourself.

  4. What happens when the system gets it wrong? safety, accountability & human oversight

    Every system can fail. Design for failure: keep a human in the loop for high-impact decisions, give people a clear way to appeal, say plainly who is accountable, and monitor the system after launch instead of assuming the test results hold forever.

!
Automation can amplify harm

One unfair decision affects one person. The same flawed rule inside a system that handles fifty thousand applications is applied fifty thousand times — identically, quickly, and often with nobody noticing.

Automation does not necessarily create the problem. What it can change is scale and consistency: the same flawed rule is applied repeatedly, quickly, and across thousands of cases, in exactly the same way every time.

The objective you choose shapes the behaviour you get

A system pursues the objective it was actually given, not the one you had in mind. If the measure does not capture what you really want, the behaviour will not either. Ask a delivery system to minimize driving time and it may route drivers through school zones at closing time. Ask a content system to maximize watching time and it may learn that anger keeps people watching. This is one of the most important lessons in this course, and you will meet it again in Module 2 under the name performance measure.

Check yourself

A university builds a model that predicts which applicants will succeed, trained on the records of past students. Name two things that could go wrong.

Show answer

One: the model repeats the past. If a certain type of student was rarely admitted before, there is little data about them and the model will rate them badly — not because they would fail, but because it never saw them succeed. Two: there is no explanation. A rejected applicant cannot be told why, and the university cannot check whether the reason is legitimate. A third answer worth full marks: predicting "success" depends on how success is defined — first-year grades, graduation, or later employment — and each definition produces a different model.

Section 1.7 optional reading

Four ways people define AI (optional)

!
This section is optional

Background reading, not part of the required material and not examined. It rounds out the picture of how the field defines itself, and you can come back to it at any time. Nothing later in the course depends on it.

The rational agent view you met in sections 1.1 and 1.2 — AI as the study of intelligent agents that perceive, decide, and act towards goals — is one of several. The many definitions in textbooks fall into a 2×2 box, and the two questions are: do we care about thinking or about acting? And do we compare the system to a human or to the ideal answer?

Our definition sits in the bottom-right box: an agent that acts to achieve its goals as well as it can.
Why "acting rationally" won

Copying human thinking is a fine goal for psychology, but a poor engineering target: we do not fully know how humans think, and humans are often wrong. "Do the action expected to give the best result" can be measured, compared, and improved. That is why every module in this course ends up asking the same question — what should the agent do next?

The Turing test, and why we do not chase it

In 1950 Alan Turing suggested a test: a judge types questions to a hidden human and a hidden machine. If the judge cannot reliably tell which is which, the machine passes. It is a famous idea and a useful thought experiment.

But engineers rarely aim at it. Passing the test rewards imitating a human, including human mistakes and human slowness. A medical system that spots a tumour better than any doctor would fail the Turing test badly — and would still be excellent AI.

Revision card

Module 1 cheat sheet

The mental model to memorize

  • An agent perceives and acts
  • Environment — what lies outside the agent and can affect it or be affected by its actions
  • An intelligent agent perceives, decides, and acts towards a goal
  • AI is the branch of Computer Science that builds systems doing tasks associated with intelligence
  • In this course's language: AI studies and designs intelligent agents
  • Several definitions exist; this course emphasizes the rational agent view
  • Quick test: does the system choose between options in order to reach a goal?
  • How to judge whether it chooses well — that is rationality, in Module 2
  • Learning is a capability some agents have — not part of the definition of an agent

Forms an agent can take

  • Software agent — acts in a digital environment
  • Robot agent — acts in the physical world
  • LLM-based agent — decides which steps and tools to use, then carries them out
  • A fixed automation workflow perceives and acts, but never decides

History in six dates

  • 1950 — Turing asks if machines can think
  • 1956 — Dartmouth workshop names the field
  • 1970s & late 1980s — two AI winters
  • 1980s — expert systems in industry
  • 1997 — Deep Blue beats the chess champion (using search)
  • 2012 / 2017 — deep learning, then the Transformer

Areas of AI

  • Search and planning · knowledge and reasoning
  • Machine learning · natural language processing
  • Computer vision · robotics
  • Areas overlap — generative AI cuts across NLP, vision, and speech
  • Each application in section 1.5 is narrow AI — built for one job or one limited domain

Responsibility checklist

  • Who could this system treat unfairly? (bias: data, design, or use)
  • Can I explain a single decision to the person affected?
  • Do I really need the personal data I am collecting?
  • What is the plan when the system is wrong?
  • Remember: the system pursues the objective you wrote, not the one you meant

Mistakes that cost marks

  • Saying AI and machine learning are the same thing — ML is one part of AI
  • Saying deep learning replaced classical AI — search and logic still run everywhere
  • Calling bias a coding bug — it can come from the data, the design, or how the system is used
  • Saying every agent is intelligent, or that an agent must be a robot
  • Calling every program that turns input into output an agent — a formula that only recalculates its own sheet is a computation
